title: TC1-08508
frame:
Forum: Refugee Appeal Division (appeal tribunal).
Parties: the appellant and the Minister; names are redacted.
How the layers nest here: The RAD member is the author (layer 1). The appellant and the Minister make submissions to the RAD (layer 2). The RPD decision under appeal is layer 3, and what the claimant or the Minister said to the RPD, as reported, is layer 4.

paragraphs.text: I dismiss this appeal. XXXX XXXX (Principal Appellant/PA), XXXX XXXX, and XXXX XXXX XXXX (Associate Appellants) are citizens of India. The Appellants fear persecution from the police in Tamil Nadu who accused the PA of receiving funding from foreign terrorist groups and being affiliated with the Liberation Tigers of Tamil Eelam (LTTE). The PA further alleges that he will be apprehended upon a return to India for violating his conditional release.

The PA alleges that he was detained for four days in 2007 by the Q Branch of the Tamil Nadu police. The PA alleges that he was then asked to come to the prison to identify two LTTE suspects but didn't go after his cousin advised him that his uncle had received the same request and did not return. The PA then travelled in England and stayed there until 2013.

The PA returned to India and reopened his XXXX business in 2013. After facing financial difficulties, he partnered with a Sri Lankan businessman who he had met in England. The PA alleges that politically connected individuals also opened a XXXX business called XXXX XXXX. In 2018, someone claiming to be from the Appellant's company made a complaint about XXXX XXXX to the police. The PA was blamed for this complaint and was assaulted and threatened as a result.

The PA was arrested by the Tamil Nadu police on XXXX XXXX, 2018. He was told that his business was supported by foreign terrorist funds. The police also asked about his friend and business partner in England, whom they alleged is a supporter of the LTTE. The PA alleges that he was detained for three days and threatened that the case would be handed over to the Q branch. The PA was released after paying a bribe, although he was required to return to the police station weekly. He and his family moved to Bangalore and went into hiding. He alleges the police came to find him at his home when he was in hiding. The Appellants then left India and travelled to Canada.

The Refugee Protection Division (RPD) found that the determinative issues were credibility and an internal flight alternative (IFA) in Mumbai. The Appellants argue that the RPD erred regarding its credibility determinations and that there is no IFA for them in Mumbai. I agree with the Appellants that the RPD erred in its credibility determinations. Nevertheless, I find that they do have a viable IFA in Mumbai.

I dismiss the appeal. The RPD was correct in finding that the Appellants are neither Convention refugees nor persons in need of protection. NEW EVIDENCE The evidence under s. 110(4) of IRPA is accepted
The Appellants are seeking to enter an article on appeal entitled "'Covid Third Wave Here Already,' Says Mumbai Mayor."

According to the law, I can only accept evidence that: (i) arose after the RPD decision; or (ii) was not reasonably available at the time of the decision; or (iii) that you could not reasonably have been expected in the circumstances to bring to the RPD before the decision.1 (iv) If the evidence meets one or more of these requirements, I must decide if the evidence is new, credible, and relevant before I can accept it.2

The Appellants are attempting to enter an article into evidence that arose after the RPD rendered its decision, given that the RPD decision was rendered on June 29, 2021, while the article is dated September 7, 2021. I find that this article is new and relevant, given that it contains information about the current country conditions in Mumbai. I also find that this article is credible, given that it appears to be an article from a reputable news source. As such, I accept this evidence into the appeal record. Oral hearing

Given that I have admitted new evidence on appeal, I must consider whether an oral hearing is necessary under s. 110(6) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act (IRPA). Having reviewed the new evidence and the record, I find that an oral hearing is not required in this appeal because the new evidence does not raise a serious issue about the Appellants' credibility that is central to the decision that, if accepted, would justify allowing or rejecting their claims.

My role is to look at all the evidence and decide if the RPD made the correct decision.3 The RPD found that credibility and IFA were both determinative issues. I will consider each of these in turn. Credibility RPD findings

The RPD found that credibility was a determinative factor in its decision. The RPD raised several issues around which it had credibility concerns, including that the PA gave vague and speculative testimony about the Q branch which it found "raises a credibility concern." The RPD also found that the PA only gave vague and speculative testimony about whether he was monitored after his arrest which "further raises the Panel's concerns as to the Claimant's credibility."

The RPD also found that the PA gave inconsistent reasons for failing to report to police following his release, whether it was because his cousin warned him that his uncle had not returned from such a visit, or whether it was because he knew several people that didn't come back from similar visit. The RPD found that his testimony was neither plausible nor credible and raised a doubt as to whether this incident ever occurred.

The RPD was also concerned about the lack of corroboration regarding the police interest in him after he travelled to the UK. When asked about police interest in him during this time, the PA testified that they asked his family about his whereabouts but there was no proof of this, as there are no records of this visit, and his parents could not provide corroboration, as they were old and it was hard for them to write as they were not well educated. The RPD noted that the PA's wife remained in their home at the time and was not persuaded that some form of confirmation of the alleged police visit from family members could not have been provided. As such, the RPD found that the PA's explanation "raises a doubt as to the alleged police visit."

The RPD further found that there was an inconsistency as to whether the authorities spoke to him or not before taking action against the XXXX XXXX. The RPD drew a negative inference as to the inconsistency in the PA's testimony on this point. The RPD also noted that, because of its "cumulative concerns as to the credibility of the claimant's allegations, the panel has some doubt as to the integrity of the claimant's testimony concerning his confrontation with XXXX owners."

The RPD noted that it had serious doubts as to the integrity of the PA's allegations concerning his jeopardy in India. However, it found that if the Appellants were concerned about their safety in Tamil Nadu, there was an IFA for them in Mumbai. Appellants' arguments

The Appellants argue that the RPD did not clearly state if it reached a negative credibility finding. Further, the Appellants argue that the RPD should have explicitly stated if their credibility was undermined and that it erred in failing to make negative findings of credibility in clear and unmistakable terms.

Regarding the RPD's concern about the PA's explanation for failing to attend the police invitation, the Appellants argue that the RPD erred in finding the PA's chain of reasoning implausible. Rather, the PA testified that his cousin had told him that an uncle of his reported to the police as requested and was never again seen. The RPD erred in failing to consider this explanation for his failure to attend.

The Appellants allege that the RPD made several credibility errors, such as finding it implausible that Indian police would invite the PA to come into the police station rather than just arresting him. The Appellants argue that there is no basis for this implausibility finding. The Appellants also argue that the RPD erroneously asked the PA to speculate regarding the actions of the agents of persecution (AOP).

The Appellants argue that the PA's evidence was generally internally consistent. Furthermore, they argue that the National Documentation Package (NDP) corroborates that the police in India are responsible for human rights abuses. Moreover, the documentary evidence notes that Indian police are corrupt and, as such, it is plausible that the PA was subject to a false arrest as alleged.

The Appellants note that the RPD found that there was an inconsistency as to whether the PA had been interviewed by authorities in relation to the complaint that was made against XXXX XXXX prior to them taking action against the company. While the PA testified to the RPD that he was not interviewed before the action occurred, he testified to counsel that he was interviewed prior. However, the PA notes that the RPD did not make a negative credibility finding on this basis. My findings

While the RPD presents several areas of testimony that raised credibility concerns, it nevertheless failed to make any concrete decisions about the consequences or outcomes of these concerns. While I acknowledge that the RPD must be careful not to prejudge any aspect of its decision, it is nevertheless incumbent on the RPD to make credibility findings that are clear and consequential. The RPD failed to do so in this case. Indeed, the RPD's credibility findings include that: a. his vague and speculative testimony "raises a credibility concern" (para. 15); b. his vague and speculative testimony about being monitored "raises ... concern as to [his] credibility" (para. 16); c. his testimony was neither plausible nor credible and "raises as [sic] doubt as to whether this incident ever occurred" (para. 17); d. his explanation for a lack of corroborative evidence "raises a doubt as to the alleged police visit" (para. 20); e. the inconsistency about whether the police spoke to him before taking action against XXXX leads the panel to draw a "negative inference as to the inconsistency in the claimant's testimony" (para. 22); f. "In the context of the panel's cumulative concerns as to the credibility of the claimant's allegations, the panel has some doubt as to the integrity of the claimant's testimony concerning his confrontation with XXXX owners." (para. 23); g. The RPD has "serious doubts as to the integrity of the Claimant's allegations concerning his jeopardy in India." (para. 26).

Based on a reading of the decision, it is abundantly clear that the RPD has several concerns about the PA's credibility. However, despite its obvious concerns, the RPD failed to explain the direct consequences of such concerns, for instance, determining that an event did not occur as alleged, or that the PA's allegations were not credible because of an accumulation of problems with his evidence. Rather, the only real credibility finding made by the RPD was when it drew a negative inference regarding an inconsistency in the claimant's testimony. However, the RPD then failed to explain the consequence of this negative inference, such as whether it was negative inference regarding the entirety of the PA's allegations, or simply a negative inference regarding the PA's testimony as it related directly to this event. Indeed, despite noting that credibility was one of the determinative issues in this case, the RPD failed to make its negative credibility findings clearly and comprehensibly as required. It is difficult to review the RPD's credibility concerns in this instance, given that its obvious concerns did not lead to consequential findings.

Nevertheless, I can review the evidence on file and reach my own credibility determination. I agree with the RPD that there was an inconsistency related to whether the PA was approached by the police before it took action against XXXX. I also find that there was an inconsistency in the PA's evidence about why he did not attend the police station when summoned, whether it was because of his cousin's warning that his uncle had disappeared under similar circumstances, or whether it was because the PA knew of several similar situations in which people disappeared. However, I do not find that these inconsistencies are sufficient to reach a finding that the PA isn't credible or to find that these events did not occur as alleged.

Furthermore, I note that several of the RPD's credibility concerns were a consequence of the speculative nature of the PA's testimony. However, it is worth noting that, in many of these instances, the RPD asked the PA questions that required him to speculate. For instance, the RPD asked the PA who told the police about his 2007 arrest (the PA named the driver and XXXX XXXX). The RPD then asked who told them about the incident (the PA stated it was local people and other sources). While the PA's responses are undoubtedly speculative, the RPD itself was asking questions about events that the PA was not present for and was unlikely to have first-hand knowledge of; as such, speculation is all he could provide. Consequently, it is unfair to discredit the PA's testimony on this basis.

I also find that the RPD erred in reaching its implausibility findings in this instance, given that the case law is clear that implausibility findings should be made only in the clearest of cases. However, the RPD's decision is unclear as to what exactly it finds implausible. I do not find that the police inviting the PA to attend the police station rather than simply arresting him is implausible. Similarly, I do not find that the PA's testimony about why he didn't attend the police station is implausible. It is unfortunate that the RPD does not explain this finding, and the alleged implausibility noted by the RPD is certainly not clear on its face. As such, this finding cannot stand.

In summary, I do not find that the RPD's credibility findings are correct in this case for the reasons noted above, and especially because it failed to specify what conclusions it drew from these concerns. Indeed, identifying these concerns is important, but it is just as important to explain the consequences of these concerns on the credibility of a given event, allegation, or the Appellant's overall credibility which the RPD failed to do.

Based on my own review of the record, I do not find that there are sufficient credibility concerns to overcome the presumption of truth. As such, I find that credibility is not a determinative issue in this case. Internal flight alternative
However, I agree with the RPD find that the determinative issue in this case is an IFA in Mumbai.

The test to determine whether a viable IFA exists has two prongs: (i) There is no serious possibility of the Appellants being persecuted or subjected, on a balance of probabilities, to a danger of torture or to a risk to their lives or of cruel and unusual treatment or punishment in the proposed IFA; and (ii) Conditions in the IFA area are such that it would not be unreasonable, in all the circumstances, including those particular to them, for the Appellants to seek refuge there.4

Once the issue of an IFA has been proposed to the Appellants, the burden is on them to demonstrate that the proposed IFA is either unsafe or unreasonable.5 Prong 1-No serious possibility of persecution or s. 97 risk RPD's findings

The RPD found that the Appellants' family had not been contacted by the AOP since their departure and that the Appellants did not have a sufficient profile to attract the interest of regional Indian police forces. It also noted that the population of Mumbai is approximately 13 million and that Mumbai is more than 1 000 kilometres from Tamil Nadu.

Moreover, the RPD noted that no evidence was tendered indicating that a criminal case had been registered in the PA's name, or that a warrant or First Information Report (FIR) had been issued. In addition, the RPD noted that the PA had no evidence of any pursuit by the police in the three years he has been away from India.

The RPD further noted that the police are under state jurisdiction, and the objective evidence indicates that there is little interstate police communication except for cases of major crime. It also found that the Appellants would not be located because of the CCTNS or their Aadhaar numbers.

Furthermore, the RPD found that there was no evidence before it that the authorities in Tamil Nadu have any interest in pursuing the Appellants or that the authorities in Mumbai have any basis to contact Tamil Nadu authorities because of any criminal information obtained. Appellants' arguments

The Appellants argue that the RPD failed to consider the PA's testimony that police continued to search for them after they relocated to Bangalore. Furthermore, they argue that the RPD erred in expecting that the police would create a FIR since they may not for many reasons. As such, the Appellants argue that the RPD erred in finding they faced no risk because they couldn't provide warrants or a FIR. Since the RPD accepted the PA's allegations, the Appellants submit that it was an error to find there was no risk because of a lack of corroborating documents.

The Appellants argue that they could be located by the AOP in this case through many methods. For instance, they argue that they would be located through tenant verification and that the police in Mumbai can do tenant verifications, and even if they don't always have the means to do it, they try.

Furthermore, the Appellants argue that political pressure is one of the reasons the police may communicate.6 Moreover, new evidence indicates that 95% of police stations are now linked to the CCTNS,7 while other country documentation notes that 14 000 police stations are now linked.8

The Appellants also argue that the RPD erred in finding that there is a viable IFA for them, given that the PA's problems are with the Q branch, which is a national organization. Furthermore, the Appellants argue that an IFA is not appropriate if you fear the police, which they do. The Appellants also argue that the police in Mumbai are also subject to political influence and corruption, and the risk they face from the police includes a risk of torture, mistreatment, and persecution.

The Appellants also argue that the RPD erred by failing to properly consider the new evidence in the June 2021 NDP in finding that it was technically impossible for the government to track citizens using the Aadhaar card.9 The country documentation suggests that Aadhaar enrolment is mandatory, and one source states that a person's Aadhaar number can be "used as a tool of surveillance."10 The Appellants also argue that the source arguing that people cannot be tracked through Aadhaar is biased, and that another source suggests that you can track someone through their name and movements. Moreover, the Appellants argue that the RPD erred in finding that the Aadhaar system had never been breached and is technically secure, given that the documentary evidence suggests that one can buy such information for as little as 10$.11 Furthermore, country documentation suggests that, since the police are not allowed to access Aadhaar, in some places the police are setting up their own databases. The Appellants argue that this is likely in Mumbai.

The Appellants argue that they will also be found because of their social media and internet use and that they would also be discoverable as taxpayers. The Appellants further argue that they would also be located through contact with their family and friends and that it is unreasonable to ask them to forego this contact and live in hiding. The Appellants further argue that they could be located via other electronic means that have been developed for tracking cases of Covid. My findings Motivation to find the Appellants unproven

I agree with the RPD that there is insufficient evidence of ongoing police interest in the PA such that there is a serious possibility of persecution for him in the IFA. Indeed, as noted by the RPD, there is no evidence before me to show that a criminal case has been registered in the PA's name in 2018, or that a warrant or FIR has been issued. I find that the police would be unlikely to conduct a countrywide search to locate the PA in the IFA when no such legal actions have been taken against him by the police. Furthermore, the PA has not provided any evidence of any pursuit or ongoing interest in him in the three years he has been away from India.

I acknowledge the PA's testimony that the police sought him once at home after he and his family went into hiding and asked his neighbours and friends about his whereabouts. However, I do not find that one attempt to locate the PA in early 2018 is sufficient to ground a finding that the police are interested in the PA such that there is a serious possibility that they would launch a countrywide search to locate him in the IFA. This is especially so since the PA and his family were able to relocate to Bangalore for five and a half months before leaving India, and there is no evidence that the police began a country-wide search for them at the time.

Having considered the totality of the evidence before me, I find that there is insufficient evidence to demonstrate that the authorities in Tamil Nadu have an ongoing interest in pursuing the PA throughout the country such that he would face a serious possibility of persecution in Mumbai. Moreover, I do not find that there is sufficient evidence before me to demonstrate that the Q branch of the police became involved in the PA's case in 2018 as alleged. While the PA was threatened with potential Q branch involvement in his case, there is no evidence before me that they became involved in the Appellant's case during his arrest in 2018 as alleged. Means and ability to locate the Appellants unproven

Furthermore, even if I found that the police were to launch a search for the Appellants throughout the country, it is not clear that there is a serious possibility that they could be located in the IFA for the reasons that follow. Location through police cooperation unproven

Even if the police were motivated to find the PA in the IFA, it would still be difficult for them to do. The objective country documentation suggests that police have a mixed record of success in tracking individuals throughout India. Part of the difficulty in tracking individuals throughout the country is because the police systems between districts and states are not integrated, which creates "[i]slands of technology" which can only communicate within a state or district.12 Furthermore, the objective country evidence suggests that regional police forces operate independently and generally only communicate to seek out individuals who have been charged with a major crime like terrorism, smuggling, and high-profile organized crime.13 As previously noted, although the PA alleges that he is a person of interest for such a crime, there is insufficient evidence before me that the PA has been charged with any such crime. Rather, the police's current interest in him would likely be because of a failure to report to the station as required, which is not a major crime such that it would result in interstate police communication.

The Appellants argue that the Q branch is a national organization, so there is no IFA. However, I note that the PA's evidence is that he dealt with the Tamil Nadu police in 2018, and that he was threatened that his case would be handed over to the Q branch by the retired police inspector who co-owned XXXX XXXX. However, it is unclear whether this handover ever occurred. Furthermore, the PA went into hiding soon after. As such, I find that there is insufficient evidence before me to find that the Q branch became involved in the PA's case in 2018 as alleged.

However, even if they did become involved, the PA's evidence speaks to the localized nature of the Q branch, in stating that the "Q Branch is part of the Tamil Nadu police."14 Similarly, the PA's evidence relating to the Q branch speaks of actions taken by "Tamil Nadu 'Q' branch sleuths."15 I do not accept the Appellants' arguments that interest in them by the Tamil Nadu Q branch means that there is no IFA for them throughout India. Rather, I find that there is insufficient evidence before me that the police involvement in this case extends to-let alone past-the Q branch in Tamil Nadu.

Furthermore, one cannot state that the whole of India is automatically unsafe for the Appellants because of the PA's interactions with the police in Tamil Nadu, even if they did come to involve the Q branch as threatened. To make such a finding would require more evidence about the Q branch and its capacity to interact with the various police districts and whether this differs from the regular interstate police communication. Barring such evidence, however, I am left to rely solely on the NDP documentation on police communication. The evidence on interstate communication is mixed and suggests that the police may be able to track and locate persons of interest depending on certain circumstances, including pressure received from political authorities. I note that the country documentation specifically states that "police authorities in India are able to track and locate persons of interest, depending on the heinousness of the crime and the pressure received from political authorities. For example, it is possible [for them] to locate a person of interest in cases of rape, murder or armed robbery."16 However, there is insufficient evidence before me to find that the PA is a person of interest in any such crimes. Rather, I find that the documentary evidence suggests that the police systems between districts and states are not integrated, and that there is no evidence before me suggesting that the Q branch in Tamil Nadu is able to transcend these issues. Location through CCTNS police database unproven

The Appellants argue that they could be located through the Crime and Criminal Tracking Network and Systems (CCTNS), given that new evidence indicates that 95% of police stations are now linked,17 with another source noting that 14 000 police stations are now linked to the database.18

The country documentation suggests that the CCTNS police database contains information on crime and criminals that interconnects police stations across the country. However, I note that the documentary evidence on the efficacy of the CCTNS is mixed, and the NDP evidence speaks to many limitations of this system. Rather, the evidence suggests that police stations in India still work in silos as far as criminal information is concerned.19 Furthermore, the evidence suggests that, despite being connected to CCTNS, "police officers ... still continue with their old ways for registering complaints and FIRs on paper."20 Indeed, while FIRs are supposed to be recorded in the CCTNS, whether and how they are recorded varies from state to state.21

Moreover, despite the numbers cited by the Appellants, the evidence continues to cite a source which states that the CCTNS is yet to become functional across the country.22 Another source states that "it has yet to become operational in the sense that the police are still not able to trace a person based on information collected under this project."23 Similarly, the documentary evidence notes that "tracking persons of interest is difficult and police have a mixed record of success."24 As such, I do not find that there is a serious possibility that the Appellants could be located in the IFA on this basis. Location through tenant verification unproven

The Appellants argue that tenant verification police checks are mandatory and could result in their being located in the IFA. They argue that the documentary evidence suggests that, even if the police don't always have the resources or ability to conduct tenant verifications, they nevertheless try.25 However, I do not find that this is an accurate representation of the specific passage cited by the Appellants, or of the country documentation more generally. Indeed, the passage cited by the Appellants notes that the police in Mumbai and other metropolises "have intermittently tried to develop a database and verify the information." However, this passage continues that "to the best of [his] knowledge, this is very inadequate and not updated regularly."26 Indeed, I find that the preponderance of the evidence suggests that such background checks are unlikely to occur. Rather, the majority of the documentary evidence in the NDP about the occurrence of this process suggests that it does not happen routinely, with a Police Commissioner in Mumbai stating that: "it is impossible for the police to actually verify the identity of all those who rent property ... the police force is not equipped to personally go and check all new tenants."27 Another source notes that the police are too ill-equipped and short-staffed to conduct such verifications when they get over 50 forms per day.28 Yet another notes that tenant verification is "extremely limited,"29 with another source stating that the tenant verification system "has several loopholes."30

As such, the country documentation suggests that, although the tenant registration system is mandatory in theory, it is quite limited in practice. Moreover, I note that the documentary evidence also cites a former deputy commissioner of police in Delhi as stating that tenant verification is "done only for the psychological satisfaction, not for actual background check [...] the cops don't make any effort to follow up with the concerned police station of other states."31

For the reasons above, I find that the objective country documentation, when considered in its entirely, suggests that there is not a serious possibility that the police in the IFA would contact the police in Tamil Nadu through the police verification process such that the AOP would become aware of the Appellants' location in the IFA on this basis. Location through Aadhaar card unproven

The Appellants allege that the RPD erred in its findings related to how they might be located through use of their Aadhaar cards. They argue that the country documentation suggests that Aadhaar enrolment is mandatory, and one source states that Aadhaar number can be "used as a tool of surveillance."32 The Appellants also argue that the source stating that it is impossible to track people through Aadhaar is biased. The Appellants also argue that the RPD failed to accept that the Aadhaar system is vulnerable to corruption, given that some evidence suggests that such information can be purchased for as little as $10.33

I acknowledge that the country documentation on tracking people through Aadhaar cards is somewhat mixed, given that, while one source states it's impossible, another source states that it can be used as a tool of surveillance. Nevertheless, as noted by the Appellants, the country documentation states that the police are not able to access this information for their investigations. As such, I do not find that there is a serious possibility that they would be located on this basis, as I do not find that there is sufficient evidence to demonstrate a that the police would break the law to access this information they are not legally entitled to use. The Appellants have also suggested that the police in Mumbai may have started their own databases. However, I do not find that there's a serious possibility that the Appellants would be located on this basis either. Rather, I find this concern to be speculative, given that there is no evidence before me that the police in Mumbai have begun to set up their own database as alleged. Furthermore, while I note that the Appellants submit that the Aadhaar system is vulnerable to data breaches, I do not find that the Appellants have shown that they could be located through their information being obtained in a data breach. They have not provided evidence to demonstrate that their data has been compromised or breached in any way. As such, their suggestion that they could be located in the IFA because of a data breach is simply speculative. Discoverable through social media, taxes, contacts, and Covid tracking

I also do not accept the Appellants' argument that they will also be found because of their social media and internet use. As noted by the Federal Court in Olusola, limitations on the use of social media are not unreasonable in a proposed IFA.34 Indeed, the Court held that it is not wrong to expect a person's use of social media to be careful, and the burden is on the Appellants to provide evidence as to how their careful use of social media would present a risk of the AOP locating them. I do not find that the Appellants have demonstrated how their careful use of social media would result in a risk of the AOP finding them in this instance. Similarly, I find the Appellants' arguments that they would be located because of their internet usage more generally to be speculative.

The Appellants also argue that they would be discoverable as taxpayers. However, I find that the Appellants have failed to provide sufficient evidence as to how the AOP in this instance would have the means and ability to locate them in the IFA through their payment of taxes.

The Appellants argue that the AOP will come to know that they are back in India if they are in contact with their family and friends and that they would have to live in hiding as a result. I find this argument is speculative. Rather, I do not find that the Appellants have provided sufficient evidence to demonstrate that they would have to forego contact with their family and friends to prevent the AOP from finding out that they have returned to India and/or where they are located. Indeed, there is no evidence before me of the AOP making efforts to contact the Appellants' friends or family to seek information about them since after they went into hiding in Bangalore in early 2018.

The Appellants have also argued that they could be located because of Covid tracking. They have provided an article that notes that all travellers coming into the state of Karnataka must register on an electronic portal which allows the state to follow them for several days. However, I note that the article states that this tracking is occurring in the state of Karnataka, while Mumbai is located in the state of Maharashtra. Consequently, I do not find that there is a serious possibility that the Appellants would be located by the AOP in the IFA because of Covid tracking. While the Appellants may wish to mitigate any perceived risk by avoiding travel to Karnataka, I do not find that such a limitation means that relocation to the IFA would be unreasonable. Similarly, I do not find that there is sufficient evidence to show that the Appellants would be required to download the government's contact tracing application such that there is a serious possibility they could be located on this basis. Summary of prong 1

For the reasons noted above, I do not find that the Appellants have provided sufficient evidence about the AOP's motivation, means, and ability to find them in the IFA such that there is a serious possibility that they could be located in the IFA as alleged. Prong 2-Reasonableness of the IFA RPD's findings

The RPD found that Mumbai is a very large multi-ethnic city and found that the PA would be likely to succeed there given that he has a high school education, business experience, and experience living in another country for a long time. The RPD also noted that the PA provided no evidence that he would have difficulty seeking and obtaining employment in Mumbai. As such, the RPD found that the PA would, on a balance of probabilities, be able to find employment in Mumbai and be able to support himself and his family. Appellants' arguments

The Appellants argue that the IFA is unreasonable because they would have to be cut off from family and friends to stay in hiding, and that they would be unable to use social media and would have to limit their internet use to hide from the AOP.

The Appellants also argue that they would be unable to work due to a significant risk of contracting Covid given the high number of cases in Mumbai. They further argue that the medical system in India is unable to cope with the pandemic and that there is a shortage of essential supplies. The Appellants also argue that the IFA would be unreasonable because they would lack access to health care, Aadhaar numbers, and a support network. My findings

I have already considered the Appellants' arguments regarding their use of social media, the internet, and contact with their family and friends. As noted above, I do not find that the Appellants have proven that they would have to be cut off from family and friends and not use social media or the internet to avoid the AOP as alleged. As such, I do not find that the Appellants have proven that the IFA would be unreasonable on this basis. Furthermore, while I accept that it could be difficult for the Appellants to relocate to an area where they do not have any family or friends close by, I do not find that the Appellants have shown that the IFA would be unreasonable on this basis.

The Appellants also argue that the PA would be unable to work due to a significant risk of contracting Covid. However, I do not find that they have provided sufficient evidence or arguments to explain why the PA would be unable to work because of Covid. Rather, I agree with the RPD that based on the PA's education and work experience, he would, on a balance of probabilities, be able to find work in the IFA. While I acknowledge the Appellants' evidence about the third wave of Covid in Mumbai having started in September 2021, I don't find that this is sufficient to prove that the PA would be unable to find work, or that it would be unreasonable for him to work in Mumbai on this basis.

Similarly, I do not find that the Appellants have shown that relocation to the IFA would be unreasonable because they would lack access to health care or Aadhaar numbers as alleged. Rather, I find that the Appellants have failed to provide sufficient evidence to demonstrate that they would be likely to have problems obtaining an Aadhaar card and basic services, including health care in the IFA. It is their burden to prove that the IFA would be unreasonable on this basis, and I do not find that they have provided sufficient evidence to discharge this burden. Rather, I find their arguments on this point to be speculative.

The Appellants also argue that the medical system in India is unable to cope with the pandemic. They have provided evidence regarding the difficulties created by Covid on the health care system, especially in Mumbai. I am mindful of this evidence and acknowledge that the evidence provided notes that the health care system is strained. However, I do not find that they have provided sufficient evidence to demonstrate that they-in their specific circumstances-would have difficulties accessing health care in Mumbai such that relocation there would be unreasonable.

While I acknowledge that there may be some difficulties for the Appellants in relocating to the IFA, a very high threshold exists for the unreasonableness portion of the IFA test. According to the Federal Court, it "requires nothing less than the existence of conditions which would jeopardize the life and safety of a claimant."35 Furthermore, it requires "actual and concrete evidence of such conditions."36 I do not find that the Appellants have provided actual and concrete evidence of any conditions that would, alone or in combination, jeopardize their lives and safety if they relocate to Mumbai. Consequently, I find that the Appellants have not proven that a relocation to the IFA would be unreasonable in their circumstances.

I dismiss the appeal and confirm the decision of the RPD that the Appellants are neither Convention refugees nor persons in need of protection.
